articles.text: Piedmont mountain climber Bill Baringer shared the chronicles of his first six climbs, to the highest peak on each continent, with the Piedmont Post. These travels were originally published in the spring of 2020 with the help of Baringer’s slideshows and travel logs. The exploits of Baringer’s climb to the top of the Australasian continent, his seventh continent, are detailed below by Baringer himself. To complete my Seven Summits journey – climbing the highest peak on each of the seven continents – I had a choice: Mt. Kosciuszko in Australia (2,228 meters, 7,310 feet – essentially the elevation of Donner Summit), or Carstensz Pyramid aka Puncak Jaya in Papua New Guinea (PNG) (4,884 meters, 16,024 feet), the highest peak in the Australasian continent. The former is achieved by taking a chairlift in the summer to the top of a ski resort, then walking an hour or two, enjoying a bag lunch, taking a couple photos, before heading home. The latter requires a helicopter flight from sea level in Timika, PNG, to a base camp at 14,000 feet – essentially the height of the tallest peaks in the contiguous United States. Mountaineers typically acclimatize after such a rapid helicopter ascent by hiking in the area Photos Courtesy of Bill Baringer Bill Baringer, at the 16,024 foot summit of Carstensz Pyramid in New Guinea on October 3, 2025.

articles.text: Editor: I am writing to ask the community to support Measure H. I’ve had the privilege of learning from great teachers at Piedmont’s schools since kindergarten. This year, my World Cultures teacher, Ms. Sohn, has had a strong impact on me. Learning about areas such as the Middle East and South America have helped my understanding of the world and current conflicts. I have learned about current disputes and where they stem from, and why solutions aren’t so easy. I find the “Picture of the Week” to be valuable: Ms. Sohn shares a picture each week from a news article; we need to identify the photo, what it is depicting, and why it is important. This has taught me about current events and given me an awareness of the world that I otherwise would not have had. Measure H is a critical funding source of our amazing schools. I hope that everyone in our community will support Measure H regardless of whether they have children. Measure H will ensure that Piedmont will continue to have great schools and teachers that can make an impact on the children of this community. –Henry Van Den Bos PHS Class of 2029
articles.title: Students in support of Measure H

articles.text: Editor: As a past Co-President of Beach Parents Organization, I’ve had the chance to see up close what makes our Piedmont schools so special, and how much that depends on strong community support. That’s why I’m voting yes on Measure H. This measure helps sustain the quality of education our kids experience in the classroom every day. I know many of us care deeply about our schools, and Measure H is a simple and essential way to protect what we value. I hope you’ll join me in voting yes. –Helen Shin

articles.text: Romi is a gentle soul who is learning the world can be a happy place. This four-yearold 45 pound sweet pittie mix simply wins people over with her tender, soulful gaze. On a recent field trip, Romi showed just how much she enjoys getting out of the shelter. She rode calmly and quietly in the car and was easy going on leash. She passed people with curiosity, noticed other dogs without reacting. While she showed interest in small animals, she moved on easily when prompted. As she became more comfortable with the volunteer, she leaned in for pets, nudged for attention, and even gave a few kisses. Romi is hoping for a calm home with a patient person with whom she can continue to blossom at her own pace. She could thrive either as your oneand-only or alongside a confident dog friend to help show her the ropes. He starts off shy, but for someone patient and perceptive, he offers the rare reward of watching trust take root and grow. When he feels safe, Thomas leans into soft petting and relaxes. You might even notice a curious glance, and you’ll melt the first time he chooses to sit nearby you. Win his heart and he’s a loyal, steady companion. This sweet boy feels most relaxed with confident, friendly cats nearby. articles.text: The Alameda Countywide Clean Water Program is offering grant applications for up to $6,000 for community-based projects that help prevent stormwater pollution and improve the health of local watersheds, creeks, and the San Francisco Bay. Eligible projects include Litter reduction efforts, public outreach and education programs, public art projects, and production of community engagement events, wildlife habitat enhancement projects, and stormwater detention. One past recipient is the Albany Landfill Dog Owners Groups and Friends (ALDOG). A grassroots volunteer community group that encourages stewardship at the Albany waterfront. They host at least three beach cleanups a year in collaboration with the East Bay Regional Park District. Their 2017 grant helped ALDOG organize a deep cleaning of the approximately 600-footlong Albany Beach. During a “Sift the Sand” event,115 volunteers removed 2,440 pounds of tiny plastic particles and other debris from Albany Beach in just one day. Another recipient was the Friends of Sausal Creek (FOSC), a volunteer-based, nonprofit organization dedicated to the restoration and protection of Oakland’s Sausal Creek and its watershed. FOSC organized workdays, student field trips, in-the-creek litter cleanups, and public trail stewardship events, engaging a total of 1,283 participants across 15 sites. The I Heart Oakland-Alameda Estuary group was a recent recipient of the grant. In September 2024, they mobilized a group of 116 volunteers to collect trash from Jack London Aquatic Center, Estuary Park, and Clinton Basin in Oakland. They gathered up 2,460 lbs of debris. The deadline for grant submissions is May 4, 2026, at 5:00 p.m. All projects must be implemented in Alameda County. For more details and to download the application packet, visit www. cleanwaterprogram.org/grants. I Heart Oakland-Alameda Estuary’s successful Earth Day cleanup. articles.text: Piedmont Council of Scouting America I am pleased to announce the selection of Tess English as Scout executive of the Piedmont Council in Piedmont, CA, effective May 16. Originally from Fairfax County, Virginia, Tess began her Scouting career in 2013 as a Pre-Professional in the Catalina Council in Tucson, Arizona, where she led the Scoutreach program serving communities across Tucson. She later advanced to Membership Specialist, focusing on new-unit development throughout the council, before serving as District Executive and then District Director for Spanish Trail District. She moved on to become District Director and Co-Field Team Leader in the Great Salt Lake Council in Salt Lake City, Utah, where she managed Bear Lake Aquatics and played a key role in guiding the council through the Stream Council in West Palm Beach, Florida. She oversaw all staff and council operations and focused on professional development, volunteer engagement, and organizational effectiveness. A proud Fox and Vigil Honor member of the Order of the Arrow, Tess is also a United States Navy veteran, having served eight years as an honored Seabee. Outside of Scouting, she enjoys spending time with family, playing rugby, and playing pick-up basketball. Within the broader community Tess serves as President of the local Kiwanis Chapter, has previously led as Chairman of the Board for the Borderland Rainbow Center, and is an active volunteer member of Fluxx Productions Inc. Please join me in congratulating Tess as she joins in partnership with the volunteers and staff of the Piedmont Council to deliver quality Scouting experiences to the young people of the communities they serve. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council unanimously voted to award a $368,053 contract to FJ&I Engineering, Inc. for the city’s Annual Sidewalk Repair Program. A total of 2,200 feet of sidewalk repairs will be made. In January this year, the council awarded a $147,557 contract for concrete shaving on offsets throughout the city. The program is continuing its repairs, moving towards the sidewalks slated for repairs that are damaged beyond what concrete shaving could fix. The city plans to remove and replace the damaged areas in the coming month. “Trips and falls are one of the major risks and liabilities any city has. We have a responsibility to identify these locations and do something about them,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzalez at the April 20 council meeting. The city plans to remove street trees that have outgrown their space and damaged the sidewalk. The city will first try to save the tree, work around it, or cut the roots. They will expand the types of trees to plant and ensure they’re tailored for warmer climates and fit the required space. “We will be looking to tailor our trees for a type of climate that will be much warmer in the future. articles.text: SAT? ACT? Should I test at all? As of today, California public schools like the UCs and Cal States are test blind, which means SAT or ACT scores are not used as part of the selection process. Some universities require SAT or ACT scores. This list has continued to grow incrementally over the past few years. The vast majority of fouryear universities within the U.S., however, continue to remain test optional. A college that is “test optional” does not require SAT or ACT scores for admission. If a student chooses to submit a score, it becomes an additional piece of information used in evaluating their application. In short, a strong SAT or ACT score could be a boon to an application! For most students, it’s worth investigating how the SAT or ACT might fit into the bigger picture. Any college that still accepts standardized test scores will take either SAT scores or ACT scores, so it’s valuable for students to get starting data points from both tests. Many schools offer the PSAT and/or PreACT to their 10th and 11th graders. Those exams are a good way to understand potential performance on the SAT and ACT. Practice tests for the SAT and the ACT are also available on their respective websites. Once a student has data from each exam, they can start thinking more broadly: How do the SAT and ACT scores compare? Are these scores on target for the schools I’m interested in or could they use some work? When should I take the test? Should I study on my own or get professional help? One of the great things about the SAT and ACT is that they are offered multiple times throughout the year, so there is flexibility around when a student can test. Students should work their SAT or ACT test date(s), and any prep they’re doing, around the things in their lives that are less flexible. For example, a student taking five AP exams in May may want to avoid taking the May SAT. For many students, the SAT and ACT are still an important part of the college admissions process but for those who plan ahead, they don’t have to be a stressful part. articles.text: Piedmont Recreation’s Play Like a Girl event returns this weekend for another actionpacked day of hands-on activities and live demonstrations with inspiring role models – all designed to get girls to consider playing sports. The event will take place Sunday, May 3, at Witter Field at Piedmont High School from 10 a.m. - 1 p.m. Aquatics sports demonstrations will take place at the Piedmont Community Pool from 10 - 11 a.m. Now in its fifth year, Play Like a Girl invites girls from 2-18 throughout the Bay Area to try their hand at sports from field hockey to flag football to roller derby. There will be 31 interactive demo stations, with guidance from skilled athletes and coaches. If a girl connects with any individual sport, there will be information available at the station about classes, leagues, and camps. Girls playing flag football at last year’s event Young girls fencing at the 2025 Play Like a Girl event Play Like a Girl will feature meet-and-greets with former WNBA player Oderah Chidom, 5-time Olympic swimming gold medalist Dana Vollmer-Grant, and other professional women athletes and Olympians. New sports this year include Badminton, Curling, Diving, Parkour, Water Polo, and Adaptive skiing. Playing sports provides lifelong benefits to girls. Participation in sports builds skills that support girls throughout their lives, teaching leadership, discipline, and teamwork. Girls who participate in sports experience lower rates of depression and higher self-esteem than their non-athlete peers. Research has shown a direct link between participation in sports and better educational opportunities, positive health outcomes, and improved career outcomes for girls: • Overall, young girls who play sports have higher grades and score higher on standardized tests than non-athletes. • Girls who participate in high school sports have higher rates of labor force participation and earn 7% higher wages than non-athlete peers. • In a 2013 study of 821 senior managers and executives, 94% of female executives reported playing organized sports after primary school. Visit piedmont.ca.gov/PlayLikeAGirl for details, to register, or to sign up to volunteer.
articles.title: Play Like a Girl event takes place May 3

articles.text: High school can be daunting, especially when you feel unprepared and anxious for what comes next. On May 2, from 5-6 p.m., Piedmont Community Service Crew is hosting a panel discussion for Piedmont Middle School eighth graders to learn more about the high school experience. The panel will be hosted in the Piedmont Middle School Multi-Purpose Room. They encourage eighth graders (and parents) to come with questions and worries about high school. A panel of six high school students, in varying grade levels, will strive to help ease 8th graders into this daunting transition. They will start with their own experiences and advice, and address burning questions that people may have. Fill out this survey (https://bit. ly/4mSbfK5) if you plan to come. Everyone is welcome, and don’t be afraid to ask questions. The Piedmont Community Service Crew is a youth-run service organization for local teens. For more information, contact Ken.i.Li@sbcglobal.net or visit their website, PCServiceCrew. org.

One of the two team finished in fourth place for their project using rice cells with the aim of reducing the dependence on synthetic fertilizers. More than 80 teams competed in the competition mostly from California. Other states and international teams, including Poland, were represented. It is the largest annual bioengineering competition for high schoolers in the country and is hosted by the UC Berkeley Bioengineering Honors Society. One team from Piedmont earned a 4th place finish for their project: “Transplanting Nitroplasts Into Rice Cells to Reduce Dependence on Synthetic Fertilizers.” The team consisted of Maximo Miller, Kalyani Spieckerman, Amelia Oldrin, and Raffaello Banin, with Sophia Tsai serving as mentor, and PHS science teacher Shelley Seto-Rosen as coach. “Not only did we develop skills in academic presentation and pitching our ideas, but we also learned through structured sessions led by undergraduate and graduate students, as well as a Forbes 30 Under 30 speaker. Exploring the many real-world applications of bioengineering truly deepened my interest in the field and left me both inspired Majid and excited about its potential to shape the future,” said Lucaccini. “I loved participating in the past seven weeks, researching a niche new discovery while exploring the field of bioengineering,” said Oldrin. “The competition offered a valuable view into what bioengineering is like in the real world. Judges offered new perspectives on aspects of our design I had never considered. I’ll definitely do it again next year,” added Miller. The team of Maya Sears, Laurel Minor, Abigail Jacoby, Leo Sachs, and Zafar Majid, put together a project titled “Microneedle Patch for Osteoarthritis Prevention and Treatment.” This team included two students competing for the second year. “Doing the competition for a second time, I felt as though I knew what to expect, but it was definitely a new experience because our solution had never been done before. Navigating how to present our solution as a device that could be marketed to a large group was the most fun part in my experience,” said Minor. “Doing this competition again was fun to focus on a new aspect of biomedical engineering, and work as a group to hypothesize a new product,” said Jacoby. “The competition was a wonderful experience. I learned a lot about what it means to prepare for and present information to judges, in a professional manner. My favorite part was touring all of the Berkeley labs. I loved researching during the past seven weeks and the process of creating a solution to a very prevalent problem,” Sears stated. Microneedle project poster

articles.text: Families enjoyed a beautiful and fun day on Thursday, April 23, at Piedmont’s Annual Arbor and Earth Day celebration at Piedmont Community Hall. The event was hosted by the Piedmont Public Works Department and the Park Commission, in partnership with East Bay Children & Nature, an Emeryville-based organization dedicated to fostering stronger connections with nature in children. The event was highlighted by the announcement of this year’s Heritage Trees. The annual event, which began in 2007, celebrates the nearly 9,000 trees the Public Works Department maintains in Piedmont’s parks and public spaces, as well as the City’s commitment to environmental stewardship. The event featured information tables hosted by the Parks Commission, Sustainability Division, and SavATree. They gave younger audiences a look into what’s inside a tree. They laid out bark and a tree trunk to showcase the rings of a tree and how to tell its age. The Park Commission handed out small plants to attendees at their table, while the Sustainability Division informed families on the proper ways to dispose of their garbage. Two professional arborists were stationed outside Community Hall to answer attendees’ plant-related questions. Children enjoyed jumping into the Public Works machinery they use daily, including the Bay Area’s first fully electric closed-circuit TV sewer inspection van. Due to ongoing unrest in the region - including terrorists firing RPGs at helicopters and taking passengers hostage - the local authorities closed the mountain on three of those arranged trips prior to my departure from SFO. After arriving in Timika on one of the attempts, the climb was cancelled the night before we were to fly to basecamp – we were all told to catch the next flight home. Walking without a police escort in Timika was strongly discouraged. On another trip to Timika, many of us waited for nearly two weeks for weather conditions to allow helicopters to fly – not only to take climbers up, but to retrieve the climbers stranded at basecamp after summiting with no alternative method of return. During that time, five climbers were trapped on the summit ridge and exposed to heavy snow and wind. Three were rescued by expedition company guides who were only still at basecamp because of the lack of heli-taxi. The two other climbers had already died in dark irony – while attempting a memorial climb to place a plaque on the mountain where their friend had perished the previous year. In October of 2025, I returned to Timika once again. Low clouds and poor weather kept us waiting in the hotels used by expedition teams. Finally, my position in the queue secured a seat for me on the first heli flight at 7:00 a.m. the next morning. My pilot managed to thread through the constantly shifting clouds and land at basecamp. The helicopter that departed just minutes after us was forced to turn back – an expensive return-tobase flight for those passengers. Forecasts suggested a narrow window: clear skies the following day, then a return to heavy cloud cover. If I spent my first day acclimatizing, I would have a spectacular climb up dry rock the next day with great views – but risk being stranded afterward. “After an hour of discussion, I convinced him that we were going to summit that day, and for him to grab his gear.” – Bill Baringer I went to the dining tent and drank as many hot drinks as I could manage, using hydration to assist my acclimatization. I then went to the guide tent and located the Indonesian guide assigned to me by the expedition company. As I expected, he told me to go rest, wander around the valley, and to take it easy. After an hour of discussion, I convinced him that we were going to summit that day, and for him to grab his gear. At first I wasn’t moving quickly, having been at sea level for an extended period. But after some time I found my rhythm and worked my way up the rock walls. In many locations, ropes had been anchored to the rocks so that a climber could use an ascender (aka Jumar) and pull themselves up the wall. In addition, given the very threadbare sections of very old rope, I wasn’t sure how much I could trust the fixed lines. The Tyrolean traverse was good fun, though at that point the weather had deteriorated and we were subjected to sleet and snow. We finally came to the point where we could climb no higher, and found the summit plaque through the very dense clouds. I quickly consumed some snacks and donned another layer of warm clothing. articles.text: Saturday, April 18 marked a historic day for Piedmont High senior Layth Haddawy. At the 2026 USPA power lifting event during Spring Break, Haddawy hit a 570 pound deadlift to set a new United States record for athletes in the Age 16-17, 148 pound category. It marked Haddawy’s first official event since winning the USPA National Championship last July, when he lifted 485 pounds. His recent lift marked an 85 pound improvement. “I did one other meet but it was just to have fun competing in the weight class above me. The deadlift is as much as the strength in your body as it is about mobility. Something I emphasized was getting as flexible as possible so I get better leverage on the bar when I’m lifting it,” Haddawy said. To achieve the mark, it took some strategic planning from Layth. He opened with a 475 pound lift, increased to 518 pounds, and followed up with 540. He then loaded up 570 pounds to beat the previous highest-mark in the U.S. of 568 pounds set in 2024. “You get three attempts per lift and are allowed to take a fourth if you’re breaking a record. I had a rough meet aside from that, and bailed 550 a week prior. I wasn’t thinking 570 was super achievable. All my warm-ups felt really light, so I talked to my coach to lower my other attempts to avoid gassing myself out. I kept my first three attempts relatively lighter so that I could get a feel if I had 570 in me,” Haddawy said. In July 2024 an MRI revealed that Haddawy was dealing with a fracture in his pelvis. He suffered an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. Photo courtesy of Get Bent Gym Layth Haddawy, a senior at Piedmont High, celebrates after setting the national deadlifting record for ages 16-17 in the 148- pound weight class. Now Haddawy said he has learned to avoid overtraining. As it turns out, it was the change he needed to better his development. Additionally, changing his diet was another big factor. “Previously, I hadn’t given much value to resting. I went to the gym almost every day and only had one rest day, and I noticed a drastic spike in my strength when I’m taking 2-3 rest days a week. I tried to focus on recovery and eating a healthier diet… My injury was another one of the reasons I incorporated more rest days. Going 5-6 times a week, I was building up inflammation in my leg, and it was impacting my mobility. My hope is to use this extra rest to mitigate the issue as much as I can,” Haddawy said. Haddawy has been training at Get Bent in Oakland since the start of his powerlifting career. PHS senior Layth Haddawy sets new national record in weightlifting By Jonathan Comeaux Saturday, April 18 marked a historic day for Piedmont High senior Layth Haddawy. At the 2026 USPA power lifting event during Spring Break, Haddawy hit a 570 pound deadlift to set a new United States record for athletes in the Age 16-17, 148 pound category. It marked Haddawy’s first official event since winning the USPA National Championship last July, when he lifted 485 pounds. His recent lift marked an 85 pound improvement. “I did one other meet but it was just to have fun competing in the weight class above me. The deadlift is as much as the strength in your body as it is about mobility. Something I emphasized was getting as flexible as possible so I get better leverage on the bar when I’m lifting it,” Haddawy said. To achieve the mark, it took some strategic planning from Layth. He opened with a 475 pound lift, increased to 518 pounds, and followed up with 540. He then loaded up 570 pounds to beat the previous highest-mark in the U.S. of 568 pounds set in 2024. “You get three attempts per lift and are allowed to take a fourth if you’re breaking a record. I had a rough meet aside from that, and bailed 550 a week prior. I wasn’t thinking 570 was super achievable. All my warm-ups felt really light, so I talked to my coach to lower my other attempts to avoid gassing myself out. I kept my first three attempts relatively lighter so that I could get a feel if I had 570 in me,” Haddawy said. In July 2024 an MRI revealed that Haddawy was dealing with a fracture in his pelvis. He suffered an avulsion fracture, which is when a fragment of bone or muscle breaks away from the main bone. Photo courtesy of Get Bent Gym Layth Haddawy, a senior at Piedmont High, celebrates after setting the national deadlifting record for ages 16-17 in the 148- pound weight class. articles.text: Piedmont to face Berkeley in WACC semifinals today Piedmont High’s girls’ lacrosse team split its last two games, bringing their record to 7-10 overall. PHS closed its regular season with a close 8-7 loss to Bishop O’Dowd on Friday, April 24, and then opened the Western Alameda County Conference postseason tournament with a 19-0 blowout of Washington. Both matches were played at Witter Field. Before the loss to O’Dowd, the Highlanders also suffered a narrow 10-7 defeat to Berkeley. They will get a chance for revenge on the Yellowjackets today, April 29, and will get another shot at the Dragons with a win at BHS. “O’Dowd crashed hard and worked really hard, they forced a lot of turnovers. They run a backer defense, which double-teams the ball every single time. A couple balls went the wrong way,” coach Carlton Chan said following their loss to O’Dowd. The losses to BOD and Berkeley came in similar fashion, where the Dragons got out to a 4-1 lead while the Jackets led 6-1 at one point. “I thought we played really well, it’s just little mistakes that build up. It ended up hurting us because it’s so high pressure. We just need to move as a team, move the ball around fast, and go full out in the first half,” senior Peyton Watson said. “It’s definitely rough to lose back to back, but now that we’ve played them, and know what to look for. We need to come out strong in the first quarter,” senior Dahlia Osman mentioned. articles.text: Visit Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery on Saturday, May 2 for a chance to step beyond the garden gates and tour Ruth Bancroft’s own private iris garden. The Iris lecture and guided tour, led by members of the Mt. Diablo Iris Society, focuses on the history of Ruth’s iris collection and how to plant, care for and divide irises with demonstrations. The Ruth Bancroft Garden and Nursery is famous for its extensive collection of succulents, cacti, California native plants, and other drought-tolerant plants. The garden was originally planted in 1972 by Ruth when it was her private, personal garden, but is now open six days a week for the education and enjoyment of the public. Ruth created a garden full of dynamic plant combinations using drought-tolerant plants that very few other gardeners were using at the time. But long before she became known for her succulents at the Ruth Bancroft Garden, Ruth was an avid iris collector. In 1989, her garden was selected by the Garden Conservancy to be its first preservation project, and a conservation easement was established to ensure its preservation. Thanks to a generous invitation from the Bancroft family, this event gives guests and garden members a rare opportunity to view her private collection. For a number of years he was the conductor of the Young Musicians’ Orchestra in Los Angeles. They played a concert in USC‘s largest auditorium. During the intermission I was backstage with Mike talking with him. As we were walking around, Mike had his jacket draped over his shoulders like a cape, and he was drinking something from a thermos when… all of a sudden…he fell face first down on the floor. His right arm flew out to protect himself. I helped him up, and he said: “I broke my arm.” The two of us were close to the stage and the stage manager said: “it’s time for the second half.” Thomas was scheduled to play a Mozart Piano Concerto and conduct the Orchestra from the piano. I gave Mike some words of encouragement and literally pushed him onto the stage. As I watched from the wings, Michael Tilson Thomas played one of the greatest concerts I’ve ever heard in my life. It was truly a super-human effort. The next day, when I saw him on the campus, he showed me the cast on his right arm and said: “I told you I broke my arm.” I replied something to the effect that…yes, his arm was broken, but that I was responsible for his brilliant performance. When I found out that Michael was ill a few years ago, I wrote to him reminding him of these memories. He appreciated the trip down memory lane. It is abundantly clear that Michael Tilson Thomas fulfilled all of the early expectations. He succeeded in every way and went on to a fabulous career… the likes of which have rarely seen. The story opens with western novelist, Monte (Morgan Freeman), disabled from a stroke, arriving at his summer cottage on Belle Island. She asks him to explain how imagination is so much a part of creating stories. And thus begins an engaging dialogue between Finn and Monte that is both literary and delightful and integral to the development of the story. Imagination also takes Monte into a dream wherein he dances with Charlotte in the moonlight, no longer confined to his wheel chair. The Magic of Belle Island reaches beyond what can seem today a coarseness of life. It is inherently hopeful in so many ways. And as a result, Monte becomes once again moored to life and purpose. articles.text: A scene from Pixar’s Toy Story 3 For all of the studio’s animated talents, and they’re considerable, Pixar (22 Oscars, four Golden Globes and three Grammys), the creators of the Toy Story franchise, have never forgotten that at the center of every project is a touching, compelling story. Since 1995, the adventures of Woody (Tom Hanks) and his crew – Buzz Lightyear (Tim Allen), Potato Heads (Don Rickles, Estelle Harris), Hamm (John Ratzenberger), Jessie (Joan Cusack), and Rex (Wallace Shawn) – have captured the imaginations of moviegoers, both young and old. Unexpectedly, the Oscar-winning Toy Story 3 delivers not only a sweet tale, one that is wonderfully imagined, but also one that is nicely distressing. Visually, it’s a treat, a smorgasbord of crisp colors and seamless animation. Put simply, it’s brilliant moviemaking. The core story is simple yet inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a daycare center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. And so begins a great adventure that is both comical and thrilling, touching on issues of loyalty, friendship, courage and seat of your pants close calls. What adults will understand is that Toy Story 3 is a coming of age story. Andy has grown up and yet still feels connected to his toys. They are, in a word, “keepers.” He can’t simply put them out by the curb. Yet he knows that he has to leave them behind in the same way he must leave his childhood (and his mother) behind. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. A doll or bear or a Woody are there, through thick and thin, and all those moments that comprise a childhood. These are wonderful themes and Toy Story 3 turns out to be the sweetest and best-told story thus far. Toy Story 3. Directed by Lee Unkrich. The core story is simple yet inspired, and immediately familiar: Andy is going away to college and is cleaning out his room. He opens up his toy box and ponders what to do with Woody and company, all deeply embedded in his childhood memories. Through a series of mistakes, the gang ends up at a daycare center run by Lots-o’-Huggin’ Bear, a seemingly nice old guy who soon proves to be something else. Kids will understand intuitively that much loved toys are to be treasured, the equivalent of a favored blanket. articles.text: Last Wednesday’s Walking on Wednesdays outing offered something a little different, a walk that traded steps for stories and scenery for stagecraft. Even with a bit of rain thinning the ranks, a solid group gathered at the Exedra and set off with purpose toward Piedmont High School, moving briskly to make the most of a special invitation. The destination was the Alan Harvey Theater, a place many in town know from performances and school events, but few have seen from the inside out. The walk down Magnolia Avenue had a sense of anticipation to it, less about distance and more about discovery. By the time the group reached campus, the pace had done its job, everyone arrived ready to listen, look, and learn. Inside, the visit began not with history, but with energy. In a drama classroom just off the main theater space, students were in the early stages of rehearsal. Music started, and suddenly the room came alive. The performance was informal, fast-paced, and full of spirit, offering a glimpse into the kind of work that rarely gets seen outside of show nights. The walkers, to their credit, stayed in their seats, resisting any urge to join in. After the brief performance, the students spoke about their work, describing not only what happens on stage but the collaboration behind it. There was talk of supporting one another, of learning timing and trust, and of the many small roles that make a production work. A student-run talent show, Phantasmagoria, is in the works, promising more of the same creativity and enthusiasm. Rebeca Posamentier greeting walkers at Alan Harvey Theater Walkers entering the Alan Harvey Theater From there, the tour shifted into the theater itself, moving from present to past. The group climbed to the upper level of the auditorium before making their way down, pausing along the way to hear about the building’s history and the evolution of the campus around it. The story begins with the original 1921 Piedmont High School, a neoclassical structure designed by architect W.H. Weeks. Its auditorium, located at the front of the building, was once a centerpiece of school life. But like many buildings of its era, it did not meet modern earthquake safety standards and was largely demolished in the 1970s. In its place came a new set of campus buildings, more modest in style but reflective of the design thinking of the time. That version of the campus did not last forever either. By the 2010s, those structures too were deemed seismically inadequate. A new chapter began with the passage of Measure H1 in 2016, a $66 million bond approved by a strong majority of voters. The goal was clear: modernize the high school, create updated learning spaces, and build a performing arts facility that could serve both students and the broader community. Construction was not without challenges. The earlier theater was removed in 2019 to make way for a new STEAM building, and only after that was completed could work begin on the current auditorium. Pandemic disruptions and rising costs forced adjustments along the way, but the project ultimately came together, opening in 2021 as a combined academic and performing arts complex. articles.text: The puppy craze may have died down since the pandemic, but there’s still a healthy market thanks to the circle of life. When choosing a new puppy, you can comb animal shelters or reach out to breeders. While many argue that “adopt don’t shop” is the way to go, there are cases where speaking to professional breeders might be more suitable, such as when interested in specific canine sports. This article specifically addresses tips and tricks for choosing a puppy when going the breeder route. First and foremost, don’t get your heart set on the first puppy you meet. Make sure you interview many different breeders and, if possible, meet several different litters of puppies. Ensure that your breeder knows the structural standards of their breed well, in addition to possible health concerns. Buyer beware if your breeder does not perform health testing or is unwilling to show you test results! When you meet your puppy, look for some important behavioral signs such as how willingly the puppy engages with their siblings as well as people. At this young stage, puppies are building their social skills, and the ideal dog will have a fondness for interacting with others. Very shy puppies can turn out to be good dogs too, however, they may need special exposure and additional training. Look for a puppy that is very comfortable being handled. Pick them up and hold them like a baby on their back – do they wiggle and try to escape or do they look lovely into your eyes? While you’re visiting, make sure you take the time to meet one or both of the puppy’s parents. Learn about their temperaments and their quirks. Are they especially friendly? Are they show dogs and if so, are they titled? A breeder who shows their dogs actively seeks confirmation from an educated professional that their dogs’ structure is excellent enough to want to pass on to their offspring. Your best chances of obtaining a healthy dog from a breeder occur when both parents have champion titles and have both gone through extensive health testing. Make sure that you are wellversed in your breed of interest so that you can recognize a scam. Many backyard breeders will attempt to pass off their practices as professional when they know very little, particularly about health conditions. If you visit a breeder who makes you feel uncomfortable, there is no shame in walking away. The puppy shopping process is a fun and very exciting time. With these simple tips, you can go through this process worry-free and paw-sitively ecstatic to welcome your new fur baby home. Sierra Berrick is a professional dog trainer and AKC Evaluator located in Oakland, California. She helped to launch the service dog and facility dog training organization Alpha Dog Assist in Mill Valley in 2021 and currently offers private training in service dog work, obedience, and behavioral consultation. To contact her, please call 510–507– 2017, email Sierra109@gmail. com, or visit her website at www. oakhillsdogtraining.weebly.com. By Cookie Segelstein Dear readers: This is not going to be a regular MacMama article, I have been asked by the editors to recount the experience of being with my mother as she was dying. Many of us have family members that are approaching the end of their lives, and though nothing can prepare us, it’s comforting to read positive accounts of the family members’ experiences as a loved one approaches the end of their lives. On January 15 of this year, I got a call from my 98-year-old mother’s memory care facility in San Francisco that she had had a small seizure and was on her way to the hospital. When I got there, she was still waiting to be seen by a doctor, and the paramedics were by her side. She was talkative, chatting with them, and basically in decent spirits considering where she was. After being there for nine hours, and after the x-rays and CAT scans, I eventually was able to talk to the physician in charge. She told me that my mom had severe pneumonia, and I had a couple of choices. She could stay there on IV antibiotics with a small chance that it would cure her, but a likelihood that this would cause delirium and incredible gastric distress with a kind of antibiotics they would have to use. The other choice was, they could try to give her some antibiotics in the ER on a drip, and then send us home with pills that most likely would not work because of the severity of her case. But there was a third choice. And that was basically to do nothing and to call in hospice. Because of my mother’s DNR wish, and her POLST that was filled out while she was still able to make decisions for herself, I knew this was the option that she would choose. And the idea of a dementia patient in the hospital hooked up to antibiotics with probable delirium was terrifying to me. I spoke with my sister, and she agreed that we would take Mom back to her apartment in the facility and make sure she was comfortable. The doctor wrote an order for me for hospice and thus began my experience and being with my mother while she died. My mother was 98, a holocaust survivor, and did very well in the memory care facility where she had lived for the last four years. The care was stellar, she was happy, she was active, and I felt very relieved that she was in a place where all her needs were covered. I visited her at least twice a week and sometimes more. In this new chapter of our lives together, I knew that the care staff would be very helpful to both of us in explaining how hospice was going to help my mother painlessly come to the end of her life. I made the decision to stop all my work and just be by her side for about 12 hours a day. In doing this, I was able to be involved with the wonderful hospice nurse in making decisions about her care as her system slowly shut down. The ER doctor told me that, even though it was impossible to predict, with the severity of her pneumonia and her white blood cell count, it would likely be a matter of about 10 days, but my mother had other plans. One of my violin students is a retired cardiologist from Johns Hopkins University. I asked him to look at my mother’s x-ray. He noted with surprise that she had “the bones of a 50-year-old”. And he also said to me something that really rang true eventually, and that is that holocaust survivors know how to survive; they don’t really know how to die. He told me not to be surprised if she lasted longer than I expected, as there is some research that shows that people who have been through starvation, can go without food longer than others. When we came back from the hospital, my mother’s food intake really was reduced, she found it hard to swallow, so I sat with her at meals so she could have that social time with her friends. We sang some songs and just visited with the other residents at her table. It was hard for her to drink water to take her pills, so they gave her thickened water, which seemed to help a little bit. Two weeks after she came back from the hospital she stopped eating completely. But she drank 4 to 8 ounces of this thickened water every day. The amazing thing is that even though her body and systems were failing, she still wanted to go to the morning activity, so we propped her up in her wheelchair, and brought her into the room where they had music, or exercise. And even though her voice was failing, she was still mouthing the words of the songs. I had no idea what to expect as far as when she would pass away, and I used Google’s AI, Gemini, and put in her vitals, her blood count, and the ER doctors’ summaries of her diagnostic tests to try to figure out what stage of death she was in. Every time I did that, it said she was nearing the final stage of death, and it gave me symptoms to look for that would indicate that she was actually very close, within hours or days. I was so surprised at how thorough the summaries were on this platform, and how helpful it was to me in preparing myself for her end. Eventually, I asked the care professionals at the facility to stop giving her regular meds because she couldn’t swallow them and just go to liquid morphine As she neared the last two weeks of her life, she had some unbelievably lucid moments. One of them was when my sister was able to come up from LA to visit her, which turned out to be the last time they were together. My mother woke up out of a deep nap, told us how much she loved us and said that she was very proud of us. For the first time in a long time, she asked how our children were by name, and told us to tell them she loves them. And then she said she knew we were here because of the situation that she is in, but she was not ready to go. She also started to see visions of her mother, and her late siblings. Or she would indicate that she saw a lot of children playing on the floor in her room. She also tried a few times to get out of bed, as she said she had to get ready. The week before she died, she had another lucid 15 minutes and said that she didn’t want to do this anymore, and she wanted to go with “the girls”. When I asked her who she was talking about, she just pointed to the door. I assumed she was talking about her sisters. At this point, she started sleeping almost all of the day, but for maybe 45 minutes of being awake. When she spoke, she mostly spoke Hungarian or Yiddish. On one of her wakeful hours, I removed the necklace from her neck, which was a little heart with a teeny diamond in it and told her that I was going to wear it. She put her hand on my neck and said, in Yiddish, “wear it in good health”. Her very last words to me were, “I’m going to sleep now”. At this point, it had been 3 ½ weeks with no food, and almost 4 days with no water. The day she died, was exactly five weeks after her visit to the ER. She died when I went to take a little walk. I was upset that I missed the actual moment of her death, but the hospice nurse assured me that many people die that way, as they can’t let go if there are family members in the room. At first, when I realized that I was going to stop all of my work, not only my MacMama work, but my violin teaching, I was very worried about my income. But I realized, I can make up that money, but I can’t make up the time spent with my mother. And because I was able to help manage her care, I was able to see that she had a peaceful and painless death with me by her side for all but the last moment. I learned a lot about the other residents in the memory care facility, how some of their family members are there often, how some of them don’t have any family members or at least don’t have any visitors. I got to know all of them, some of them wandered into my mother’s room occasionally, one woman in particular, another holocaust survivor, who spoke Hungarian, used to hold my mother’s hand and sing to her. I went to the activities with them, I went to arts and crafts with them, I had meals with them, I became part of their community just for those five weeks. The experience of being able to be with my mother as she left this life is something I will never forget, and I am eternally grateful that I made the choice to take the time to do that. It has made my grieving much easier, and I really learned to appreciate the caregivers that spend their days doing the work of caring for the elders in our families.

People from all over the Bay Area were able to grab food originating from kitchens across the globe and then sit and enjoy an equally diverse array of entertainment. Food Fest founder Roger Tsai was once again heavily involved in the event’s production, bringing together talent and food trucks for one special day. “When I started Piedmont Food Fest back in 2022, I just hoped to have enough vendors, entertainment, and guests to make it worth everyone’s time. After that first one, I realized there was a collective excitement around celebrating the many cultures we have in the Bay Area through food, drinks, and music,” said Tsai. Tsai gave credit to the hundreds of volunteers who supported his vision to expand the festival and make it an even greater celebration. “To celebrate our fifth year milestone, we wanted to bring an even greater variety of food, drink, and entertainment to the festival,” Tsai continued. “Pulling off this vision required over 100 volunteers to plan, promote, and operate the many parts of the day, and I’m really proud of how our team showed up to deliver a memorable day for all.” The KidZone & Craft Stations were organized by Kala Hale, Abha Kothari, Sarah Eisemon, and Laura Edeen. Hundreds of kids spent their time playing at ten different carnival booths and enjoyed the favorite sno-cone station. The area was run by volunteers from the middle and high school, covering four shifts. Nine community groups and local businesses set up tables to advertise their services. These groups ranged from charity efforts to fun group activities for attendMaikaze Daiko put on a professional Japanese taiko performance. A performer of Beloved Aerial Arts dances in the sky for the passerbys to enjoy. A blindfolded Han Martial Arts master kicks roses into the crowd. The empanadas were a crowd favorite. The crowd paid close attention to the wonderful performances on the main stage. The World Harmony Chorus provides a peaceful performance for the crowd. The wine and microbrewery tasting zone ees to sign up for. In addition, a beer and wine tasting provided 13 microbreweries and wine options for older guests to enjoy. Food Fest guests had the option of many different cultural foods, including Thai, Vietnamese, and Japanese, all in front of the Exedra. Further down the hill, guests had the choice of Moroccan, Mediterranean, seafood, Spanish, Japanese desserts, soul food, and Indian food. Further options included smoothies, boba tea, poke, shaved ice, and empanadas. This reporter sampled the Nepali food truck Momolicious, and tried their Fiery Mo:mo: and Mango Lassi. At $20, the meal featured Crispy stir-fried dumplings with sweet-and-spicy sauce, onions, and bell peppers, while the drink served as a sweet reward to deal with the heat. In front of Piedmont’s vase at the Exedra, talented acrobats from the “Beloved Aerial Arts” performed while suspended in midair with three hours of graceful entertainment. Over the last five years, Food Fest has become an event that those around the Bay Area look forward to for its county fair-style entertainment and a superb selection of menus.
